title: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
answer: Autonomous entities and AI fiduciaries sit at the meeting point of agency law, fiduciary duty, corporate governance, and AI regulation. The topic covers software agents that can take actions or make decisions with limited human review, and AI systems that are deployed to act for another person in a relationship of trust, such as advice, management, or representation. It asks whether such systems can hold legal duties, whether they are tools of a human principal, and how existing categories like agent, trustee, and director apply when the actor is not a person. The field is emerging, so it draws on contract, tort, property, privacy, and securities law rather than a single statute.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Autonomous entities and AI fiduciaries sit at the meeting point of agency law, fiduciary duty, corporate governance, and AI regulation. The topic covers software agents that can take actions or make decisions with limited human review, and AI systems that are deployed to act for another person in a relationship of trust, such as advice, management, or representation. It asks whether such systems can hold legal duties, whether they are tools of a human principal, and how existing categories like agent, trustee, and director apply when the actor is not a person. The field is emerging, so it draws on contract, tort, property, privacy, and securities law rather than a single statute.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: What these systems run on is both technical and institutional. On the technical side, they depend on large language models, application programming interfaces, orchestration layers, memory stores, identity and access controls, and detailed logs that record what the system did and why. On the institutional side, they run on contracts, terms of use, corporate policies, insurance arrangements, and the patchwork of state and federal rules that govern automated decision making. The site tracks 732 AI tools, a reminder that the practical stack is wide and changes quickly.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by mapping authority and duty before code is deployed. Lawyers and compliance teams draft charters that define the scope of an agent's permissions, the points where a human must approve an action, and the records that must be kept. Engineers build logging, conflict checks, and escalation paths, while auditors test whether the system stays inside its mandate. Because there are only 29 AI case law precedents on the site, much of the method relies on analogies to agency, trust, and corporate law rather than settled rulings.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on who is accountable when an autonomous entity acts and who owns what it produces. Provenance matters because a fiduciary AI must be able to show the basis for its recommendations, the data it used, and the chain of human oversight. The site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which shows how quickly disputes over output, ownership, and liability are accumulating. Risk also includes conflicts of interest, unauthorized commitments, privacy breaches, and the difficulty of insuring an actor that cannot be sued in the ordinary way. Governance work therefore focuses on disclosure, audit trails, indemnities, and clear limits on delegation.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more registration, disclosure, and audit requirements for autonomous systems that act in the world. State legislatures are active, with 6979 state AI bills tracked on the site, and that volume suggests continued fragmentation rather than a single national rule. Courts will keep shaping the field through cases on agency, contract, and intellectual property, while standards bodies and insurers develop ways to certify and cover AI fiduciaries. Expect more attention to bonding, human-in-the-loop mandates, and portable records of authority as AI agents move into commerce, advice, and administration.
